title: Exports hit record in Sept., nine-month earnings at all-time high | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 27 October 2026 02:10
-     - 14

Sri Lanka’s export sector posted its highest-ever monthly performance in September 2026, with total earnings surpassing $ 1.69 billion and reflecting a 17.23% year-on-year (YoY) growth driven by strong merchandise shipments, despite the challenges faced by the tensions in the Middle East and its direct impact on overall costs.

The latest data released by the Sri Lanka Export Development Board (EDB) showed that merchandise exports shipped in September were up 21.66% YoY to over $ 1.38 billion, though estimated service earnings in the month showed a moderate growth of 0.67% YoY to $ 306.17 million.

The September exports registered a 5.6% month-on-month (MoM) increase compared to August 2026.

Cumulative exports during the first nine months of 2026 rose by 5.04% YoY to over $ 13.61 billion, also marking the highest recorded level for the period.

Merchandise export earnings during January-September increased by 5.35% YoY to over $ 10.76 billion, whilst services exports during the same period were estimated to have surged by 3.88% to $ 2.85 billion. Services exports include sectors such as ICT/BPM, construction, financial services, and transport and logistics.

Addressing the media, EDB Chairman and CEO Mangala Wijesinghe described the September outcome as a resilient way towards achieving the country’s annual merchandise export target of over $ 18 billion, whilst commending exporters for navigating external shocks and yet contributing to economic development.

“This performance demonstrates the potential of Sri Lankan exporters to strengthen their presence in international markets despite an increasingly competitive global trading environment. As we move forward, our priority must be to sustain this growth momentum by strengthening the competitiveness of existing export sectors while accelerating the development of new products, services and markets,” he said.

For 2026, Sri Lanka has set an ambitious export revenue target of $ 20 billion, reflecting an anticipated YoY growth of 10-12%. Merchandise exports are expected to exceed $ 15.7 billion in 2026, while services exports are projected to rise to $ 4.3 billion.

The EDB noted that the merchandise exports growth in September was driven largely by improved demand across the agricultural and industrial product categories, while services lagged. 

Apparel and textile exports rose 3.46% YoY to $ 439.78 million in September 2026, from $ 425.07 million a year earlier. Exports to the US rose 6.33%.

Rubber and rubber-based product exports surged 33.68% to $ 99.31 million, up from $ 74.29 million in September 2025. Industrial and surgical rubber glove exports grew 34.38% to $ 31.70 million, while pneumatic and retreaded tyres and tubes increased 39.57% to $ 54.95 million.

Exports of spices, essential oils and oleoresins climbed 73.19% to $ 74.73 million. Pepper exports jumped 165.38% to $ 23.46 million, while cinnamon exports rose 68.27% to $ 42.59 million. Coconut fibre-based product exports recorded a 2.99% increase.

Activated carbon exports grew 43.52% YoY to $ 25.26 million, reflecting stronger earnings from value-added coconut-based products.

Food and beverage exports increased 27.92% to $ 63.77 million in September 2026, compared with $ 49.85 million a year earlier. Electrical and electronic component exports surged 88.35% YoY to $ 68.54 million, supported by a 114.62% increase in insulated wire and cable exports.

Seafood exports rose 4.01% to $ 23.61 million, from $ 22.70 million in September 2025. Frozen fish exports increased 15.85% to $ 13.96 million, while shrimp exports surged 207.27% to $ 3.38 million.

Meanwhile, transport and logistics services exports were estimated at $ 167.9 million, up 23.32% from $ 136.15 million in September 2025.

Cumulative export earnings from key value-added sectors recorded YoY growth during January–September 2026. Rubber-based products rose 8.44%, coconut-based products 3.68%, processed food and beverages 20.9%, electrical and electronic components 61.05%, and spices and concentrates 30.53%.

However, apparel and textile exports declined 5.68% YoY to $ 3,783.76 million. Apparel exports fell 5.36% to $ 3,513.37 million, while textile exports dropped 9.66% to $ 270.39 million. Exports to the US, European Union (EU) and the UK decreased by 3.83%, 5.54% and 10.41%, respectively, amid subdued demand in key markets.

Tea export earnings fell 6.83% to $ 1,083.58 million. Tea packet exports declined 4.42%, while bulk tea earnings dropped 11.13%. Growth in tea bag exports of 53.39% and instant tea exports of 9.85% was insufficient to offset the overall contraction.

Weaker demand in the Middle East further affected performance, with tea exports to the region falling 34.22%. Shipments to the United Arab Emirates, Iran and Iraq declined by 59.66%, 65.80% and 47.72%, respectively.

The US, Sri Lanka’s largest export market, accounting for 20.3% of merchandise exports, recorded an 18.06% YoY increase in September 2026, with earnings reaching $ 281.84 million. Cumulative exports to the US rose marginally by 0.05% to $ 2,252.99 million during January–September 2026.

India overtook the UK to become Sri Lanka’s second-largest export destination, with cumulative exports increasing 12.3% to $ 889.84 million during the first nine months of 2026. September exports to India surged 29.65% YoY to $ 113.22 million. In contrast, exports to the UK fell 3.17% to $ 71.71 million in September, while cumulative earnings declined 9.33% to $ 654.36 million.

Exports to the EU, accounting for 20.12% of Sri Lanka’s merchandise exports, increased 1.92% YoY in September 2026. However, cumulative exports to the bloc declined marginally by 0.15% during January–September 2026, indicating broadly stable performance in the key market.

title: BOC to raise up to Rs. 30 b in  Sri Lanka’s largest-ever listed debt issue | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 27 October 2026 02:07
-     - 13

Bank of Ceylon (BOC), Sri Lanka’s leading state-owned commercial bank, is set to create another milestone in the country’s capital market with the launch of Sri Lanka’s largest-ever listed debenture issue, with a maximum issue size of Rs. 30 billion.

The bank proposes to initially raise Rs. 10 billion, with an option to increase the issue to Rs. 20 billion in the event of an oversubscription of the initial tranche and a further option to increase the total issue size up to Rs. 30 billion, making it the largest listed debenture issue undertaken in Sri Lanka.

The proposed issue comprises Basel III compliant, Tier 2, Listed, Rated, Unsecured, Subordinated, Redeemable debentures with a non-viability write-down feature. The debentures carry an issue rating of AA (Stable) from Lanka Rating Agency, while BOC’s issuer rating stands at AA-(lka)/Stable from Fitch Ratings Lanka Ltd.

The debentures will be offered with five-year and seven-year maturities, providing with medium to long-term fixed income investment opportunities. The issue is confined to qualified investors and the minimum subscription for qualified investors is Rs. 10,000, while individual investors are required to apply for at least Rs. 5 million. 

The debentures are offered in four different types to meet diverse requirements of qualified investors. The fixed coupon rate of the five-year debenture will be 12.75% per annum while the floating coupon rate will be 1.50% above the applicable twelve-month Treasury Bill rate. The Fixed coupon rate of the seven-year debenture will be 13% per annum while the floating coupon rate will be 1.75% above the applicable twelve-month Treasury Bill rate.

BOC’s largest debenture issue comes at a significant juncture for the Sri Lankan economy, at a time when the country is prioritising sustainable, investment-led and inclusive economic growth. Against this backdrop, a stronger capital base will further enhance BOC’s capacity to mobilise and channel funds towards productive sectors of the economy, thereby supporting Sri Lanka’s next phase of economic development. This landmark issue therefore represents more than a significant capital-raising exercise for the bank. BOC, as the country’s leading state-owned commercial bank, remains well positioned to play a pivotal role in financing businesses, facilitating investment and supporting the broader development priorities of the country.

BOC is a Corporate Finance Advisor licensed by the Securities and Exchange Commission of Sri Lanka. This largest Basel III Debenture issuance was exclusively structured and managed by the Investment Banking team who possess a wealth of expertise in structuring innovative capital market instruments. The issue follows BOC’s pioneering Sustainability Bond issuance, another landmark transaction structured and managed by the bank’s Investment Banking Division, reflecting BOC’s continued leadership in developing innovative capital-market solutions while advancing sustainable finance in Sri Lanka.

The Legal Department of BOC acts as the lawyers to the issue, while the Corporate Branch of the bank acts as the bankers to the issue. The Investment Banking Division will also continue to act as the Registrar to the proposed issue, while Hatton National Bank PLC will be the trustee to the issue.

The bank is opening the subscription list of the BASEL III Debenture Issue at 9.30 a.m. on 3 November 2026 and will remain open for 14 market days unless the bank decides to close it earlier based on subscription levels.

Applications for the debentures will be accepted from qualified investors in accordance with the terms and conditions set out in the Prospectus. The Prospectus and application forms can be downloaded from the web sites of the CSE; www.cse.lk and BOC; www.boc.lk.

Duly completed application forms should be enclosed in an envelope marked “BOC Debenture Issue” together with the remittance for the full amount payable on application and delivered to the Investment Banking Division at 7th Floor of BOC Head Office or collection points mentioned in the prospectus.

With a long-standing presence in Sri Lanka’s banking industry, Bank of Ceylon has played a significant role in the country’s economic development by mobilising savings, extending credit and supporting individuals, businesses and major economic sectors. The proposed debenture issue is expected to further enhance the bank’s capacity to support corporate, SME, retail and institutional customers while maintaining prudent regulatory capital buffers.

Investors are advised to carefully read the Prospectus, including the terms of the debentures, risk factors, non-viability write-down provisions and eligibility requirements, before making an investment decision.

Bank of Ceylon invites eligible local and foreign investors to participate in this landmark issue and be a part of the bank’s continuing journey of financial strength and contribution to Sri Lanka’s economic development. At a time when the country is entering a new phase of investment-led growth, the issue represents an opportunity for investors to participate in the growth journey of the nation’s leading state-owned commercial bank while contributing to the broader economic progress of Sri Lanka.

title: Mark Surgenor wins historic BCC International President’s Award 2026 | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 27 October 2026 02:06

Council for Business with Britain in Sri Lanka President Mark Surgenor

In a groundbreaking achievement on the global business stage, Mark Surgenor, President of the Council for Business with Britain (CBB) in Sri Lanka (2023–2025), has been named the winner of the British Chambers of Commerce (BCC) International President’s Award 2026.

Out of a competitive international network of more than 75 British Chambers of Commerce and Business Councils worldwide, this recognition marks a monumental milestone as the first time ever that Sri Lanka has received this prestigious award.

The annual Chamber Awards celebrate the individuals and organisations that strengthen the global Chamber Network and drive international commerce.

Mark...

Surgenor was specifically honored for modernising the CBB during his two-year presidency (2023–2025), successfully transforming it from a traditional networking group into a high-value platform for commercial insight, trade access, and strategic connections.

His tenure included hosting high-impact forums, engaging with over 200 member organisations, and founding CBB NextGen - a structured platform empowering the next generation of business leaders and entrepreneurs. Surgenor is CEO of HSBC Sri Lanka and Maldives.

 Additionally, he significantly strengthened bilateral partnerships with the British High Commission, the UK Department for Business and Trade, the Ceylon Chamber of Commerce, and peer councils.

Commenting on the award, Surgenor said: «I›m honoured to receive the President›s Award and hugely grateful to everyone across the Council who has contributed to what we›ve achieved. Together we›ve worked to strengthen UK-Sri Lanka business links, bringing the next generation into our work and ensuring the Council offers real value to its members.»

British Chambers of Commerce President Andy Haldane, CBE added: «Mark›s leadership shows the difference one individual can make to an entire business community. He has modernised the Council and created stronger practical connections between firms in the UK and Sri Lanka. This award is thoroughly deserved recognition of his energy, integrity and lasting contribution to the global Chamber Network.»

Award supporter Quest CEO Des Shaw said: «Mark has combined strategic vision with practical delivery, creating lasting value for members and ensuring the Council is well placed for the future. We warmly congratulate him on his achievements.»

To read the official announcement from the British Chambers of Commerce, visit: British Chambers of Commerce News

title: India says port expansions no zero-sum game for Colombo | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 27 October 2026 02:04
-     - 15

India’s drive to build its own transhipment hubs is not playing out at Colombo’s expense, a leading Indian maritime strategist said, pointing to global shipping lines now investing in ports on both sides of the Palk Strait.

New Delhi-based National Maritime Foundation (NMF) Director General Vice Admiral Pradeep Chauhan said port connectivity, long a source of anxiety in Sri Lanka, had become the most promising area for maritime cooperation between the two countries.

He was speaking at the 50th webinar organised by the Daily FT, ACCA and the International Chamber of Commerce Sri Lanka, together with WIM, the Sri Lanka Institute of Directors, the MBA Alumni Association of the University of Colombo and Pioneer Institute of Business & Technology, on Saturday. The webinar was titled “In an Emerging New World Order, What Are Sri Lanka’s Options?”

“In India and Sri Lanka, there has been a concern that as India develops its own transhipment hubs, will Colombo suffer?” Vice Admiral Chauhan said. Transhipment is the transfer of cargo from one vessel to another at an intermediate port en route to its final destination, and forms the core of the Port of Colombo’s business.

He said the concern stemmed from how two Indian initiatives were viewed: the maritime policy encapsulated in the acronym SAGAR, and Sagarmala, which he described as India’s mega port connectivity initiative. For a while, in some minds, the two had pulled in opposite directions, with one seeking inclusivity and the other seen as excluding partner countries from the circulation of Indian money, he said.

“But now I think that this is an area, peculiarly enough, which is the most promising for maritime cooperation, and it is already happening,” he said.

Pointing to the major shipping lines, Vice Admiral Chauhan noted that Mediterranean Shipping Company (MSC) had decided to invest in both Colombo and Vizhinjam, which he described as the Indian port directly competing with Colombo. “This is not playing out as a zero-sum game. Far less is it playing out as a gloom and doom story,” he said, adding that it was an area in which a much greater amount of intellectual capital needed to be invested. Coastal shipping, he said, formed part of the same activity.

His view was echoed by former Sri Lanka Navy Commander Admiral Jayantha Perera, who said Colombo, a global transhipment hub, drew about 80% of its transhipment cargo from India. “So there’s no competition with India. We have to cooperate with India and we must improve our level,” he said, adding that only then could Sri Lanka win the confidence of global shipping.

Admiral Perera said Colombo handled about 9.9 million twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs), the standard measure of container volume, with capacity expected to reach about 11.1 million TEUs with the East and West terminals and about 15 million TEUs with expansion by 2028. Shipping density around Sri Lanka had risen sharply due to the Middle East conflict, with vessels at times having to wait outside port, he said.

Beyond ports, Vice Admiral Chauhan identified disaster response as an area in which India and Sri Lanka were natural partners, “even if for no other reason than misery loves company”, and called for cooperation on human skilling so that human skills augmented rather than were threatened by AI, an area he said was receiving insufficient attention.

He also urged a shift from treating the blue economy as a set of sectors to the “blueing” of the entire regional economy, saying Sri Lanka in many cases held the key, such as in converting shipping, a large polluter, into a greener mechanism by running smaller craft that ply between India and Sri Lanka on electricity rather than fossil fuels.

title: PDMO rejects all Domestic Dollar  Bond bids; market says bid rates too high | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 27 October 2026 02:03
-     - 10

The Public Debt Management Office (PDMO) has rejected all bids received at its Domestic Dollar Bond auction held on 23 October, with market sources indicating that demand was encouraging, but the rates bid were too high.

The issue was for $ 100 million, with the option of raising up to $ 300 million. “Pursuant to Section 6 of the Offer Document, which reserves the Issuer’s right to accept or reject any application, in whole or in part, the Issuer has decided not to accept any bids received under this auction,” the PDMO said in its notice, giving no further details.

The fixed rate of interest payable on the bonds, which are US dollar-denominated debt securities issued in the domestic market, was to be determined through competitive bidding.

Market sources said the PDMO probably believed the bids did not factor in Fitch Ratings’ recent upgrade of Sri Lanka.

In September, Fitch upgraded Sri Lanka’s Long-Term Issuer Default Rating to ‘B-’ from ‘CCC+’, with a Stable outlook. A higher rating typically lowers the risk premium investors demand over benchmark US Treasury yields, which together determine dollar bond pricing.

Given the availability of funds and current global uncertainties, the PDMO may be willing to wait before returning to the market, the sources said. Accepting costlier bids could also have set a higher benchmark for future foreign currency borrowing.

This was the second Domestic Dollar Bond issue since the debt crisis. In the first, in December 2025, the PDMO raised $ 50 million under a fixed-rate arrangement, recording firm demand for one- and two-year maturities. The one-year tranche drew $ 45.5 million in bids, of which $ 33 million was accepted at a weighted average fixed rate of 5.7%. The two-year tenor received $ 42.5 million in bids, with $ 17 million accepted at a weighted average rate of 6.1%. Only $ 1 million was bid for the three-year maturity, and no bids were accepted.

title: Japan pledges over Rs. 600 m for Kelani River water quality project | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 27 October 2026 02:02
-     - 9

Japan has pledged over Rs. 600 million for a five-year project to monitor and improve water quality in the Kelani River basin, with the first consignment of water testing equipment handed over to Environment Minister Dr. Dammika Patabendi yesterday.

Implemented through the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) and the Japan Science and Technology Agency (JST) under the SATREPS program, the 2026-2030 project will set up a basin-wide monitoring network and an aquatic environment data platform to collect and analyse water quality information, supporting evidence-based Government policymaking.

It will also develop policy frameworks, train personnel, engage technical experts and publish research findings.

Japanese representatives handed over the equipment at a steering committee meeting at the Central Environmental Authority (CEA) auditorium. It was then distributed among the CEA, the University of Moratuwa and General Sir John Kotelawala Defence University. The University of Moratuwa’s Aquatic Environment Data Operations Centre will play a key role in implementation.

The 145 km Kelani River, with a basin of about 2,300 sq. km, is a major source of drinking water for Colombo and surrounding areas. Approximately one-fourth of Sri Lanka’s population lives in the basin, which has 14 major water treatment and distribution facilities and more than 5,400 industries, including CEA-authorised operations in the Biyagama and Seethawaka industrial zones.

The river faces significant pollution from industrial wastewater, untreated sewage, agricultural waste, and sand and gem mining, while floods and droughts also affect water quality. There are no specific groundwater quality standards either, a concern as groundwater is a major source of drinking water for many Western Province households.

Environment Ministry Secretary K.R. Uduwawala leads the steering committee, while Tohoku University Prof. So Kasama is principal investigator. The meeting was attended by JICA representatives, CEA Chairman Prof. Tilak Hewawasam, CEA Director General Kapila Rajapaksa, University of Moratuwa Department of Civil Engineering Prof. Lalith Rajapaksa, the Kaduwela Municipal Commissioner and Environment Ministry officials. The Department of Irrigation, the Water Resources Board and the Clean Sri Lanka Secretariat are also involved.

The project aims to lay a scientific foundation for water quality management across the basin, with the goal of ensuring safer drinking water for the public by 2030.

title: Laugfs Gas weighs stake sale in Hambantota LPG terminal | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 27 October 2026 02:02
-     - 11

Laugfs Gas PLC yesterday said it was in preliminary, informal discussions with interested parties on strategic options for its wholly owned subsidiary Laugfs Terminals Ltd., including the potential disposal of part or all of its shareholding.

Laugfs Terminals owns and operates the 30,000 MT liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) terminal at the Hambantota International Port. The options under consideration include commercial collaboration, investment and a potential partial or full sale of the company’s stake in the subsidiary.

No agreement has been reached on the structure or terms of any transaction, and no definitive transaction agreement has been entered into, the company said, adding that there was no certainty the discussions would result in a transaction. Accordingly, any financial impact could not be determined at this stage.

The company said it would promptly disclose material developments in accordance with the Colombo Stock Exchange Listing Rules.

title: Sumathi Holdings celebrates 70 years of success | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 27 October 2026 01:54
-     - 7

Sumathi Holdings marked its 70th anniversary on 9 October, with a celebration at the Sangam Ballroom of ITC Ratnadipa, Colombo, attended by over 500 guests from Sri Lanka’s business, government, financial and media communities. 

Held under the theme “70 Years of Sumathi Legacy”, the evening looked back to 1956, when founder Mr. U.W. Sumathipala opened Sporting Star’s first betting shop on Maliban Street, Pettah – the business from which the Group grew.

The evening opened with a drone show and fireworks over Galle Face. The program that followed included an address and toast by Chairman Jagath Sumathipala, the unveiling of the 70th anniversary logo, and addresses by Directors Chadu Sumathipala and Chathula Sumathipala, accompanied by a live orchestra and performances by vocalist Umara Sinhawansa, pianist and music director Soundarie David Rodrigo, and composer and singer Nadeeka Guruge.

U.W. Sumathipala built Sporting Star into one of the country’s leading bookmakers and established it as the market leader. He also expanded into cinema, supporting the growth of the Sri Lankan film industry and into gems, representing the business at The World Gem and Jewellery Exhibition in Milan. His values of “Honesty and Integrity” remain the Group’s guiding principles today.

After U.W. Sumathipala’s passing in 1979, Jagath Sumathipala joined the business at the age of 19, supported by his maternal uncle, Dharmasiri, who guided him in the horse racing operations. His first assignment was to create the Group’s own race paper, which he turned into a commercial printing company. He moved the main office from Maliban Street to Chatham Street and carried forward his father’s gem business. When his brother, Thilanga Sumathipala, returned from his studies in 1986, Jagath Sumathipala handed the racing operations over to him, and Thilanga Sumathipala built them further.

In 1987 took a new step, Jagath Sumathipala opened Sri Lanka’s first race-by-race live commentary betting shop. Building on this, the Group began broadcasting races in 1992 and by 1998 was showing every race live across all its outlets. Today Sporting Star operates more than 200 outlets across the island and, since 2019, the online platform BetSS.com.

Milina Sumathipala’s influence reached well beyond the business. She gave the entire profit of her film Ganga Addara (1980) to build a Neurosurgery Unit at the Colombo General Hospital, today’s National Hospital. In 1981, she began the blood donation drives and support for the Cancer Hospital through which more than 20,000 pints of blood have since been donated, and in 2001 she became the first woman President of the All Ceylon Buddhist Congress.

Following a restructuring in 2017, Jagath Sumathipala, together with the third generation, has shaped Sumathi Holdings into a Group of 11 principal businesses employing more than 2,000 people, across betting and gaming, healthcare, information technology, restaurants, security, printing, renewable energy, investments and film.

Much of today’s Group began as an answer to something Sporting Star needed. Security for its outlets became Lokx Security Services; printing for its racing papers became InPrint Solutions; and the technology behind its betting systems is now developed by Mainframe.

Three Group companies mark milestones of their own this year:

Great Wall Restaurants turns 35. Jagath Sumathipala set it up in 1991 on Chatham Street to bring authentic Chinese food to Colombo.

Sumathi IT turns 25. It provides network infrastructure, data communications and geospatial engineering across Sri Lanka, and introduced DJI’s enterprise drones to the country.

LifeServ turns 25. The healthcare distributor has been a leader in Sri Lanka’s drug-eluting stent market for two decades and opened an oncology division in 2025.

A third generation now leads the Group alongside the Chairman. Chadu Sumathipala leads the Group’s IT sector: he founded Mainframe, brought the Group’s key systems in-house, built BetSS.com, and set up Sumathi IT’s drone division and its first research and development centre. Chathula Sumathipala leads the Group’s services cluster and grew LifeServ built Sumathi Energy, whose projects include the 5MW Wewila solar plant and battery storage at Monaragala and Wewila.

The celebrations extended to the Group’s people. On 8 October, Sporting Star’s head office celebrated with its staff and presented long-service awards to more than 200 employees with ten or more years’ service, 31 of whom have been with the company for over 30 years. The longest-serving, R.V. Ghanasena of Anuradhapura, has been with Sporting Star for 40 years. On 10 October, Sporting Star outlets across the island held celebrations of their own for staff from Great Wall Restaurants and commemorative gifts for customers.

Sumathi Holdings Chairman Jagath Sumathipala said: “Seventy years ago, my father opened a single shop on Maliban Street, built on his word and the trust of his customers. Honesty and integrity built this Group, and the more than 2,000 people who stand with us today carry those values forward. As we enter our eighth decade, our commitment is to build the businesses that will serve Sri Lanka for the next seventy years.”

title: OPA presents collective professional proposals for Budget 2027 | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 27 October 2026 01:53
-     - 10

The Organisation of Professional Associations of Sri Lanka (OPA), under the leadership of OPA President Jayantha Gallehewa, presented its proposals and recommendations for the Budget 2027 to Treasury Secretary Dr. Harshana Suriyapperuma at a meeting held on 6 October, 2026.

The proposals represent the collective voice and professional expertise of the OPA’s 52 member associations, bringing together knowledge and perspectives from across Sri Lanka’s professional community. The initiative was undertaken through the National Issues Committee (NIC), chaired by OPA Vice President and NIC Chairman Bhanu Wijayaratne, with the active contribution of its members.

The proposals were developed through consultations with the OPA’s member associations and focused on key areas of national importance, with the objective of providing constructive and evidence-informed recommendations to the national Budget process.

Among the key areas addressed were fair taxation, export financing, elder care and social protection, research and innovation, the circular economy, the built environment and heritage, and measures to address the country’s professional brain drain. The proposals also reflected wider professional perspectives on strengthening economic resilience, improving productivity, encouraging investment and supporting sustainable national development.

The OPA delegation was led by OPA President Jayantha Gallehewa and included General Secretary Eng. Ravi Rupasinghe, Vice President and NIC Chairman Bhanu Wijayaratne, NIC Member B.A.H.S. Preena, OPA Assistant Secretary Indika Ranaweera, Vice President and Career Guidance and Skills Development Committee Chairman V. Rameshkumar, NIC Member and Career Guidance and Skills Development Committee Convener Udesh I.W. Seneviratna and OPA Editor Priyantha Wickramarathna.

Speaking on the occasion, Gallehewa emphasised the organisation’s commitment to placing the knowledge, experience and collective expertise of Sri Lanka’s professional community at the service of the nation. He noted that the OPA’s role extends beyond representing individual professions and includes contributing constructively to national policy and decision-making.

The presentation of the Budget proposals marks another important step in the OPA’s continuing engagement with the Government. Through the NIC and its 52 member associations, the OPA continues to provide a platform for translating professional knowledge and experience into practical recommendations on matters of national importance.

The OPA expressed its appreciation to the Finance, Planning and Economic Development Ministry for providing the opportunity to present its proposals and reaffirmed its readiness to continue contributing professional expertise to the national development and Budget process.

title: UNP demands immediate presidential pardon for Gnanasara Thera | Daily FT

The United National Party (UNP) yesterday demanded an immediate presidential pardon for Ven. Galagodaaththe Gnanasara Thera, facilitated by the intervention of the Maha Nayake Theros of the Three Chapters, to resolve the ongoing crisis.

In a statement, the party said the Sathyagraha, a non-violent sit-in protest, demanding the Thera’s release had been suspended following a notification by the Maha Nayake Theros.

Citing former Chief Justice Sarath N. Silva, the UNP said the maximum prison sentence for contempt of court was 18 months, and that Gnanasara Thera had already served more than 10 months in prison for the offence.

The party said steps had previously been taken to secure a presidential pardon for the Thera at the request of the Maha Nayake Theros, and claimed that the Supreme Court ruling had indicated another presidential pardon could be considered.

The UNP also criticised the Government for obtaining court orders against Buddhist monks who had not taken part in the protest march and Sathyagraha demanding the Thera’s release, describing the move as a serious mistake. It further called for an investigation into those responsible for ordering the removal of the Thera’s robes.

title: Sajith discusses proposed  anti-terrorism, organised  crime laws with diplomatic corps | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 27 October 2026 01:58
-     - 10

Opposition Leader Sajith Premadasa has met representatives of diplomatic missions and international organisations in Colombo to discuss concerns over proposed legislation targeting terrorism and organised crime. 

According to a statement issued by the Opposition Leader's office on 25 October, the discussions focused on the proposed Protection of the State from Terrorism Bill and the Prevention of Organised Crimes Bill, with particular attention to their potential impact on fundamental rights, judicial independence and constitutional protections.

Former parliamentarian M.A. Sumanthiran, along with serving and former lawmakers, also expressed concerns about the proposed laws during the meeting.

Premadasa said legislation to combat terrorism and organised crime was necessary, but stressed that such measures must be accompanied by effective judicial oversight and safeguards to prevent the misuse of executive powers.

The discussions also addressed objections raised by the Human Rights Commission of Sri Lanka (HRCSL), which warned in a statement issued on 21 October that the proposed Prevention of Organised Crimes Bill was “wholly incompatible” with the fundamental rights provisions of the Constitution and the country’s international human rights obligations.

The Commission cautioned that the proposed law could be more draconian than the Prevention of Terrorism Act of 1979 and called for its withdrawal and substantial revision.

Key areas of concern included; provisions permitting confessions to senior Police officers, detention authorised by the executive, broad definitions of serious offences and limitations on judicial discretion in decisions concerning remand and bail.

The HRCSL has separately called for revisions to the proposed terrorism legislation, urging the authorities to adopt a narrower definition of terrorism, ensure judicial supervision of detention orders, guarantee access to legal representation and strengthen safeguards governing bail.

The Bar Association of Sri Lanka (BASL) has also called for the withdrawal of the proposed organised crime legislation and the withdrawal or amendment of the terrorism Bill in its current form.

Premadasa urged the Government to make the recommendations of expert committees’ public and conduct broader consultations with the HRCSL, the BASL and other relevant stakeholders before proceeding with the legislation.

He said constitutional safeguards were important not only for politicians and activists, but also for ordinary citizens who might come into contact with the criminal justice system.

title: Supreme Court enters decisive judgement in relation to jurisdiction of Commercial High Court | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 27 October 2026 01:57
-     - 11

A bench of the Supreme Court comprising Justices Mahinda Samayawardhena, Dr. Sobhitha Rajakaruna, and K.M.G.H. Kulatunga delivered judgement overturning an order of the Commercial High Court on 21 October, by which the Commercial High Court had dismissed an action at the pre-trial stage on the basis that there was insufficient evidence to establish the claim to satisfy the minimum monetary threshold of the Commercial High Court to hear a case.

According to the order of the Commercial High Court which was challenged, the position taken up by the Defendant that the Plaintiff’s claim had been artificially inflated to meet the jurisdictional threshold of the Commercial High Court was upheld by the Commercial High Court also with a finding that there was no evidence placed to support the claim. The Defendant in the case had initially raised a jurisdictional objection on the basis that the dispute was not a commercial dispute as there was no written contract or agreement between the parties. However, at the pre-trial stage, the Defendant had altered its objection and contended that the monetary threshold had not been met. Having considered the objections raised by the Defendant, the Commercial High Court dismissed the Plaintiff’s entire case in 2024.

The Plaintiff-Appellant, Kish International Ltd., thereafter preferred an appeal to the Supreme Court, contending that the transaction between the parties was intended to be in USD and that, cumulatively, the sums claimed in the Plaint including demurrage, loss of profits, and interest exceeded the statutory threshold required to file the case in the Commercial High Court as demonstrated in the Plaint. It was the Plaintiff-Appellant’s position that the Commercial High Court could not lawfully dismiss the action at the pre-trial stage on the ground of an alleged lack of evidence as the pre-trial hearing is not the stage at which evidence is led or evaluated. The Appellant further contended that the High Court Judge ought not to have permitted the Defendant to reformulate a jurisdictional objection that had not been pleaded in the original defence.

Justice Samayawardhena, in the judgement of the Supreme Court, specifically addressed, inter alia, the role of the pre-trial conference, which constitutes a pivotal stage in civil proceedings: “The purpose of the pre-trial conference is not to provide an opportunity for a party to introduce a new case outside the scope of the pleadings, to expand the scope of the dispute, or to prepare the case for a full-fledged trial.”

The Supreme Court further held that “jurisdiction cannot ordinarily remain in suspense throughout the proceedings and ultimately depend upon the result of the very adjudication which the Court assumed jurisdiction to undertake. If jurisdiction is properly attached when the action was instituted, a subsequent finding on the merits that the Plaintiff has proved an amount less than that claimed does not, for that reason, retrospectively divest the Court of jurisdiction.”

In addition, the Supreme Court, in its judgment, held that Parliament had used the word ‘including’, which should be given a wider interpretation, encompassing ‘commercial transactions’, and providing guidance as to the nature and breadth of the transactions that Parliament intended to bring within the jurisdiction of the Commercial High Court. It was held that the expression ‘commercial transactions’ must be given a broad and purposive interpretation, rather than being confined to the particular categories expressly enumerated in item 1 of the enacting act.

The Supreme Court observed in its judgement that the Commercial High Court Judge had required the Plaintiff, at the pre-trial stage and before the action had even been fixed for trial, to establish by evidence the several components of its claim which the Supreme Court contended was a matter for determination upon the evidence at the trial. It was held that the absence of evidence establishing a particular component of the claim at the pre-trial stage could not justify the conclusion that such amount should be excluded in determining the pecuniary jurisdiction of the Court.

The Supreme Court through this extensive judgement proceeded to set aside the impugned order of the Commercial High Court and awarded costs against the Defendant-Respondent in respect of both the proceedings before the Commercial High Court until the dismissal and the Supreme Court appeal. The Supreme Court further directed the Commercial High Court to proceed with the matter and to hear and conclude the case expeditiously.

On behalf of the Plaintiff-Appellant, Kish International Ltd., Counsel Nishan Premathiratne appeared with Vikum Jayasinghe and Manith Dasanayake on the instructions of Gamindu Karunasena.

The Commercial High Court was firstly established in 1996 by an Act of Parliament and it is presently holden in the Western Province to hear and determine disputes of a commercial nature above Rs. 50 million, including matters relating to intellectual property, admiralty, debt recovery and arbitral referrals.

title: Digital VAT in Sri Lanka: Why platform liability and reverse charge are essential to avoid costing households and Treasury | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 27 October 2026 01:46
-     - 12

Executive summary

Sri Lanka’s VAT on cross-border digital services, in force since July 2026, is a necessary and overdue reform, but its design is incomplete. It relies only on registration by non-resident suppliers and fully carves out supplies to VAT-registered businesses. Without platform liability and a B2B reverse charge, it will likely under-collect and place the entire new burden on households.

Key points

Background: The reform was IMF-backed, with a modest expected yield (0.04-0.08% of GDP). Its stronger case is equal treatment of local and foreign suppliers. It was delayed twice before Act No. 14 of 2026 confirmed the July start.

Weak enforcement: The Inland Revenue Department would have to chase foreign vendors with no local presence. Large brands may register, but smaller providers likely won’t.

B2B carve-out: (Supplies made to local VAT registrants): Reverse charge would raise real revenue from banks, financial institutions, life insurance companies and other VAT registered companies who are prevented from claiming full VAT input credit, which are exempt from invoice-credit VAT and therefore cannot claim input tax credits under that mechanism, while also creating an audit trail. The carve-out forgoes this, loses visibility, and leaves local providers at a disadvantage.

Equity: Individuals pay digital VAT while businesses buying the same services pay nothing, which undercuts the aim of base broadening and any future cut to the 18% rate.

Global practice: Simplified registration for B2C supplies and reverse charge for B2B supplies are widely used internationally. Platform liability is also increasingly adopted, including in the EU, UK, Australia, Canada and Singapore, but its scope varies. OECD guidance presents platform liability as an effective policy option. 

Recommendation: Keep simplified registration for B2C supplies, add platform liability for marketplaces, app stores, and replace the B2B carve-out with reverse charge. Support these with clear location-indicator guidance, proportionate penalties and data-sharing with financial institutions.

Completing the framework with platform liability and reverse charge

Sri Lanka’s decision to tax cross-border digital services represents a necessary and overdue modernisation of the Value Added Tax system. It responds to the reality that value is increasingly created and consumed online, often without any physical presence in the country of consumption. 

Local providers have long charged VAT on comparable services while many non-resident suppliers have not. The reform aims to correct that imbalance, broaden the tax base, and support the eventual possibility of reducing the high 18% standard rate.

 Yet the framework that has been enacted relies almost exclusively on vendor registration by non-resident suppliers and contains a complete carve-out for supplies to VAT-registered businesses. This design is incomplete. Without the addition of platform/marketplace liability and a reverse charge mechanism for business-to-business supplies, the regime risks delivering only a fraction of its potential revenue while placing the entire incremental tax burden on individuals and households. Policymakers still have the opportunity to strengthen the legislation and the accompanying administrative rules so that digital VAT becomes a genuine instrument of base broadening rather than a limited and largely symbolic measure.

A record of ambition tempered by repeated delay

The intellectual and policy origins of digital VAT in Sri Lanka are well documented. The International Monetary Fund’s June 2024 staff report identified the taxation of digital services as one element of a broader package intended to raise revenue and improve neutrality. The expected yield was modest, approximately 0.04% of GDP in the first full year, with some estimates ranging up to 0.08%. The stronger argument was never the absolute size of the revenue but the principle of equal treatment: a Sri Lankan consumer purchasing streaming, software or cloud services from a foreign provider should face the same VAT treatment as one purchasing from a local supplier.

Legislative progress followed a familiar pattern of announcement, enactment and postponement, further prolonged by a Supreme Court challenge that delayed the regime’s finalisation and exacted a real opportunity cost in foregone revenue. The Value Added Tax (Amendment) Act No. 4 of 2025 was certified on 11 April 2025. Gazette Notification 2443/30 of 1 July 2025 set an original effective date of 1 October 2025. Cabinet subsequently deferred implementation to 1 April 2026. A further postponement moved the start to 1 July 2026. The Value Added Tax (Amendment) Act No. 14 of 2026, certified on 30 June and published in gazette on 3 July 2026, finally placed the regime on a firm statutory footing and confirmed the July 2026 commencement.  

Although Sri Lanka’s digital-services VAT provisions came into effect on 1 July 2026, with section 25L principally governing registration and section 25N providing that VAT is not charged where the recipient is VAT-registered, the regime remains non-operational in practice because the prescribed registration form has yet to be made available, preventing non-resident digital service providers from completing the registration process.

The mechanics that emerged are conventional in outline but incomplete in substance.

Non-resident suppliers of digital services through electronic platforms must register once their supplies to persons in Sri Lanka exceed Rs. 60 million in any twelve-month period or Rs. 15 million in a quarter. A recipient is treated as located in Sri Lanka if at least two of the following indicators are present: a billing or residential address in Sri Lanka, payment through a Sri Lankan bank or financial institution, a payment instrument issued in Sri Lanka, or a Sri Lankan IP address. Registration, return filing and payment are electronic; payment may be made in Rupees or an approved foreign currency, either directly or through a representative. Supplies to VAT-registered resident businesses are entirely carved out. No obligation is placed on platforms, marketplaces or app stores to collect or remit VAT on the underlying supplies they facilitate.

Digital VAT: Real revenue, not a compliance checkbox

This sequence of delays and the final design choices invite a sober assessment. Digital VAT should not be reduced to a compliance checkbox required by an external program. It should raise meaningful revenue, follow the proven architecture used by successful jurisdictions, and contribute to the larger project of base expansion that can eventually support a lower standard rate. Features that work elsewhere should not be discarded because of lobbying pressure, administrative convenience or incomplete understanding of implementation options. More than one hundred countries already collect VAT on non-resident digital services. The tax base belongs to the country of consumption. Sri Lanka is entitled to collect it fully.

Introducing marketplace liability and reverse charge would convert a half-measure into a credible instrument of fiscal policy, one capable of raising revenue, promoting fairness between local and foreign suppliers, and supporting the longer-term objective of reducing the high standard VAT rate of 18% that currently weighs on consumers. The tools exist. International experience demonstrates that they work. The remaining question is whether Sri Lanka will choose to use them

OECD recommendations and the global standard

The OECD International VAT/GST Guidelines, together with subsequent practical toolkits, provide the clearest international consensus on how to tax cross-border supplies of services and intangibles. For business-to-consumer supplies the recommended approach is to require the non-resident supplier to register and account for the tax under a simplified regime. For business-to-business supplies the preferred mechanism is reverse charge: the local business customer accounts for the VAT as if it were the supplier.

This arrangement relieves the foreign supplier of registration obligations on those particular supplies while ensuring that the tax is reported and, where the customer cannot claim full input credit, that revenue is actually collected. Where digital platforms facilitate the transactions, the OECD strongly encourages jurisdictions to impose liability on the platform itself—the “deemed supplier” or full platform liability model. Platforms already possess customer location data, control payment flows and can scale compliance far more efficiently than a tax administration attempting to locate and compel thousands of individual foreign vendors.

International practice is not uniform. Simplified vendor registration for B2C supplies and reverse charge for B2B supplies are widely used across jurisdictions. Platform liability is also increasingly adopted, including in the European Union, the United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand, Canada and Singapore, but its scope differs. OECD guidance identifies platform liability as an effective policy option.

Australia’s extension of GST to imported digital services and the European Union’s progressive introduction of deemed-supplier rules illustrate the practical advantages of concentrating collection at the platform level. Enforcement becomes realistic, the long tail of smaller suppliers is captured, and revenue leakage is substantially reduced.

Sri Lanka’s exclusive reliance on vendor registration, the absence of platform liability, and the substitution of a full B2B carve-out for reverse charge constitute the weakest available combination of collection methods. Large, reputation-conscious global brands may eventually register. The multitude of smaller software providers, freelance platforms, content creators and niche applications almost certainly will not. The Inland Revenue Department will be left to pursue entities that have no local presence, no local bank account and little commercial incentive to comply. When the same administration already faces well-documented challenges in securing full compliance from resident taxpayers, the expectation that it can effectively police non-residents who simply ignore registration or under-declare values is unrealistic. 

Platform liability reverses the burden of enforcement: a limited number of large, visible platforms become the collection points, using systems and data they already maintain.

The revenue and equity cost of the B2B carve-out

The decision to exempt supplies to VAT-registered businesses rather than apply reverse charge carries particularly serious consequences for both revenue and fairness. 

Under a reverse charge mechanism a local VAT-registered recipient self-assesses the tax. For a fully taxable business the net cash effect is neutral because the output tax is matched by an equal input credit. Banks, financial institutions, life insurance companies and other VAT registered companies who are prevented from claiming full VAT input credit are subject to the separate VAT on financial services but are exempt from invoice-credit VAT; accordingly, they cannot claim input tax credits under the invoice-credit mechanism. The same concern may arise for other businesses whose ability to recover input tax is restricted. Those sectors are significant purchasers of foreign cloud computing, software licenses, digital advertising, data analytics and related services. Reverse charge would therefore generate genuine additional revenue from a rapidly growing category of imports. It would also create a complete audit trail that allows the tax authority to monitor the volume and nature of cross-border digital purchases.

Under the B2B carve-out, the foreign supplier does not charge VAT and the VAT-registered recipient does not self-assess it. However, the enacted framework may still require the foreign supplier to furnish prescribed information concerning such supplies to the Inland Revenue Department. The carve-out therefore does not necessarily leave these transactions entirely unreported, but it does not create the same recipient-level self-assessment and audit trail that a reverse charge would provide. This limits visibility and may make misclassification, for example, a private consumer presenting as a business is more difficult to detect.

Local digital service providers continue to charge VAT while their foreign competitors do not on B2B sales, recreating the competitive distortion the reform was intended to eliminate.

This outcome stands in direct contradiction to the stated policy objective of base broadening. Broadening the tax base cannot mean capturing only individuals, households and non VAT registrant businesses, while excluding businesses that are exempt from invoice-credit VAT, including banks, financial institutions, life insurance companies and other VAT registered companies who are prevented from claiming full VAT input credit, from the reverse-charge net. Yet that is the practical effect of the present design. 

Individuals, households and non VAT registrant businesses pay digital VAT on streaming subscriptions, applications, software and online services. Businesses purchasing comparable or identical services from non-resident suppliers face no corresponding liability. The entire additional burden of expanding the VAT base in the digital sphere therefore falls on ordinary consumers. Such an arrangement is inequitable. It is also fiscally short-sighted. Every Rupee of revenue left uncollected from B2B digital imports is a Rupee that cannot contribute to the fiscal space required for a future reduction in the standard 18% rate.

Fairness, administrative capacity and the question of influence

The present design raises uncomfortable questions of fairness. 

Domestic VAT registration thresholds have been subject to repeated adjustment; more local small and medium enterprises face compliance obligations and the associated costs. At the same time the largest global platforms face only a registration form that they may or may not complete, with no marketplace liability to enforce collection on the many underlying suppliers they host. Local providers charge VAT; foreign providers of B2B digital services do not. The competitive playing field remains tilted.

It is legitimate to ask whether the abandonment of reverse charge and the omission of platform liability reflect purely technical judgment or the successful representation of interests that prefer the current, limited arrangement. 

Reverse charge, by its ordinary operation, would have brought businesses exempt from invoice-credit VAT, including banks, financial institutions, life insurance companies and other VAT registered companies who are prevented from claiming full VAT input credit, into the collection mechanism and produced revenue that the carve-out simply forgoes. Administrative convenience is not a sufficient justification for forgoing that revenue. Other countries with larger digital markets and more complex economies have implemented the fuller OECD package. Sri Lanka does not need to invent new systems. It can adapt existing models and begin with the largest platforms. 

The alternative, proceeding with vendor registration alone and a full B2B carve-out, almost guarantees modest receipts, persistent non-compliance among smaller foreign providers, zero contribution from the B2B segment, and, within a relatively short period, another round of legislative amendments to correct what could have been designed correctly from the outset.

A practical and proven path forward

A more robust framework is available and does not require radical innovation. It would retain simplified electronic vendor registration for business-to-consumer supplies, introduce platform liability for major marketplaces, app stores, and replace the B2B carve-out with a reverse charge mechanism. 

Supporting measures, clear guidance on the application of location indicators, proportionate penalties, and structured information exchange with financial institutions would complete the architecture. These are precisely the tools that have proven effective in other jurisdictions. They align with OECD recommendations, protect the competitive position of local providers, generate revenue from purchases by businesses exempt from invoice-credit VAT, including banks, financial institutions, life insurance companies and other VAT registered companies who are prevented from claiming full VAT input credit, and ensure that base expansion is not borne solely by households.

Sri Lanka cannot afford a digital VAT regime that exists primarily to satisfy an external checklist. The digital economy is one of the few expanding tax bases available to the country. Confining collection to vendor registration while carving out the entire B2B segment is, in effect, planning for underperformance. Policymakers still possess the authority and the time to strengthen the regime before it settles into underwhelming practice. 

Introducing marketplace liability and reverse charge would convert a half-measure into a credible instrument of fiscal policy, one capable of raising revenue, promoting fairness between local and foreign suppliers, and supporting the longer-term objective of reducing the high standard VAT rate of 18% that currently weighs on consumers. The tools exist. International experience demonstrates that they work. The remaining question is whether Sri Lanka will choose to use them.

(The author was awarded Tax Practice Leader of the Year 2024 (ASPAC) by International Tax Review (ITR) and was a top-four finalist for Tax Litigation and Disputes Practice Leader of the Year (ASPAC))

title: Mango Tree test of Arahat Mahinda | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 27 October 2026 01:38
-     - 15

Before preaching Buddhism to King Devanampiya Tissa, Arahant Mahinda used a logical puzzle — often described as the world’s first recorded intelligence or wisdom test — based on a mango tree to check if the king had the intellectual capacity to understand the Dhamma

Age and a frail heart keep me confined to my home, yet an alert mind keeps me voraciously curious.

Two private TV channels—both epitomising the vulgarity of free-market capitalism—keep me updated on the Sangha mischief in our public square. Pensive in my armchair, far removed from the calibrated, boorish ‘Bana’ at the Satyagraha sit-in at Viharamahadevi Park, my mind drifted into a desperate daydream.

I closed my eyes and wondered: What if? What if the time warp separating antiquity from today’s chaos were ripped open, and Arahat Mahinda Thero himself stepped out of the third century BC and onto the soil of twenty-first-century Sri Lanka?

What if the legendary missionary son of Dharmasoka walked among us today, only to find that his pristine, liberating message of the Buddha had been weaponised, commodified, and reduced to pageantry and ritual, making the cry of ‹Sadhu’ an agitational refrains of hired hooligans?

It was a mind-boggling possibility: the architect of Sinhala Buddhism surveying how a capricious, power-hungry priestly class had traded the profound logic of the Mihintale mango tree for luxury SUVs, political contracts, and televised circuses.

In this mental theater, the ancient sage Arahat Mahinda had come to interrogate, wielding the sharp intellect that once founded a nation to utterly dismantle the pious fraud of its modern guardians.

Arahat Mahinda Thero stood at the Satyagraha protest site. Under a canvas canopy, a group of saffron-clad figures sat in a single row, striking poses of deep, meditative exhaustion for a cluster of television cameras.

This was the grand satyagraha, orchestrated at the behest of a defunct political dynasty whose members are currently adrift, desperate to reclaim their lost turf.

Shrouded in simple, earth-toned robes, my imaginary Arahat Mahinda stepped straight out of the third century BC and into the chaotic theater of this modern political circus.

He had no entourage, no media coordinator to assist him; he walked directly to the enclosure where the main architects of this spectacle sat.

The test 

There sat Ulapane Sumangala, adjusting his microphone with practiced ease; Balangoda Kassapa, frantically checking his smartphone under the fold of his robe to see if his latest TikTok live-stream was trending; and Walanhanduwe Dharmaratna, the High Priest of Mihintale, looking noticeably uncomfortable so far from his mountain rock sanctuary and so close to actual public scrutiny.

The trio blinked, squinting through the camera glare. There was something terrifyingly authentic, something fiercely primordial about the visitor that rendered their haughty air of entitlement suddenly very fragile.

Hoping to capture a viral moment of monastic solidarity, Ulapane Sumangala cleared his throat, assumed a pose of pious pain, and bellowed into the microphone: “Welcome, Most Venerable Arahath Therun-wahanse, to our sacred struggle!”

The transient political circuses built by greed are nothing more than passing shadows on the ever-changing landscape of time. They do not define our beautiful island, nor can they ever truly compromise the pristine core of the Dhamma. For twenty-three centuries, the true light brought by Arahat Mahinda has endured—not through golden fences, luxurious pageants, or the patronage of powerful politicians, but because the pristine Dhamma resides quietly and immovably within the hearts of ordinary, virtuous people

Sumangala proclaimed, his voice booming through the speakers: “We sit here in noble sacrifice to save our nation, our heritage, and our Sasana from the treacherous hands of those who demand accountability and transparency!”

The imaginary Arahat Mahinda looked at the elaborate sound system, the stock of bottled mineral water tucked behind the cushions on which the ‹Satyagrahis› sat, and the fleet of SUVs parked on the roadside behind the marquee.

A faint, razor-sharp smile touched his lips. He did not recite a stanza, nor did he offer a conventional blessing. Instead, he pointed a calm, steady finger toward a large, leafy tree standing nearby.”

 “Monks,” Arahat Mahinda said, his voice carrying a thunderous, resonant clarity that dwarfed the loudspeakers. “What tree is that?” he intoned.

 Monk Walanhanduwe Dharmaratna, recognising the opening lines of the famous logic test that his own monastic perch had on our free-market economy, perked up.

He saw an immediate opportunity to demonstrate his scriptural authority. “That, Most Venerable One, is a mango tree.”

“Are there other mango trees besides this one?” Arahat Mahinda inquired, his demeanor glistening with sharp, deductive intensity.

Age and a frail heart keep me confined to my home, yet an alert mind keeps me voraciously curious.

“Yes, Most Venerable Arahath Therun-wahanse,” Balangoda Kassapa chimed in, eager to display his intellect to his digital followers. “There are many other mango trees in this park, and indeed, across the entire island.”

“And are there trees here that are not mango trees?” asked Arahat, his voice tightening like a bowstring.

“Of course, of course!” Ulapane Sumangala joined the fray, sensing a rhetorical victory. “There are Mara trees, Na trees, and many majestic banyans. There are countless trees that are not mango trees.”

Arahat Mahinda paused. A sudden, dramatic silence overwhelmed the entire park. The wind ceased to blow. The birds stopped chirping. Then he leaned forward, his gaze flashing like lightning: “Apart from those other mango trees, and the trees that are not mango trees, does this specific mango tree itself remain?›”

“Naturally, Venerable Sir!” Monk Walanhanduwe Dharmaratna answered confidently. “If you set aside all other mango trees and all non-mango trees, this solitary tree still stands right where it is. It is elementary!” responded the Mihintale custodian.

Arahat Mahinda’s face hardened, shifting from calm inquisitor to Cosmic Arbiter. “An excellent grasp of basic botany. Now, let us apply this same rigorous line of reasoning to the political forest you have planted here today. Tell me, Sumangala, who are the people currently funding, supplying, and cheering for this noble satyagraha of yours?”

Sumangala puffed out his chest, adopting a fiercely theatrical posture. “These are the righteous guardians of the old order, Sir! The visionary leaders who built great expressways, the generous patrons who gave us unchecked power, and the elite statesmen currently unjustly sidelined by the ungrateful masses!”

 “I see,” Arahat Mahinda, the Ashokan envoy, replied smoothly, his tone dripping with sarcasm. “And are there other corrupt, discredited politicians in this country besides the ones who paid for your tents, your cheer squads, and your ears today?”

Kassapa shifted uneasily, his phone buzzing violently in his palm as the live comments started flying in. “Well... yes. History is full of them. There are many political opportunists across the land who have plundered the public purse.”

“And are there people in this country who are not corrupt, discredited politicians?” Arahat pressed further, his voice rising to a crescendo.

Portly Monk Walanhanduwe Dharmaratna coughed into his hand, looking nervously at the cameras that were now capturing his sudden panic. “Yes, technically. The vast majority of the citizenry are ordinary, hardworking people who simply wish to live in peace, feed their children, and see justice prevail.”

The imaginary Arahat Mahinda of my daydream stepped onto the stage, his presence making the Satyagraha space feel suffocatingly small.

 ‘Then tell me, wise monks,’ Arahat Mahinda roared, his authoritative voice shaking the very poles of the makeshift tent. ‘If we set aside all those other corrupt politicians roaming elsewhere, and if we set aside the entire population of honest, hardworking citizens who want nothing to do with your theater... who is left sitting under this tent?!’”

“An absolute, terrifying silence stilled the air. Television cameras zoomed in on the sweat breaking out on Sumangala’s brow. Arahat Mahinda’s deductive trap had snapped shut with the force of a steel jaw. By their own logic, the only entities remaining in the equation were the handful of compromised oligarchs pulling their strings, and the monks who consented to act as their spiritual human shields.

‘You see,’ Arahat Mahinda continued, his voice dropping to a devastatingly sharp whisper that cut deeper than a blade, “Twenty-three centuries ago, I used this very riddle to ensure that a king possessed the logical capacity to govern for the welfare of all living beings. I taught him that the land belongs to the people, and that the ruler is merely its temporary guardian. But you three have completely inverted Dhamma! You have become the vanguard of brazen rogues, using the sacred robes of the Enlightened One to protect the hordes of the greedy!›”

 “Venerable Sir!” Walanhanduwe protested, his face turning an angry shade of crimson as he clutched his relic casket for comfort.

“We are protecting our traditional privileges! If the elite fall, who will sponsor our grand pageants? Who will build our golden fences? Who will pay for our luxury hybrid SUVs?!”

 “The Dhamma does not require a golden fence built with stolen public funds!” the resonant voice of the Arahat replied, firm as the Mihintale rock. “A true sanctuary is built on virtue, not on the patronage of a discredited court. Look at yourselves! You call this a satyagraha firm adherence to truth. Yet your truth is bought by the plateful, your fasting is a comedic illusion staged between television commercial breaks, and your devotion is a transactional lease signed with politicians currently adrift in the turbulent currents of their own bad karma!”

Balangoda Kassapa quietly slipped his phone into his bag, suddenly very aware of how utterly ridiculous his live-stream looked to a nation laughing hysterically in the comments section. Ulapane Sumangala tried to rally his thoughts to launch a fierce counteroffensive about external conspiracies and threats to their heritage, but the words withered in his throat, completely vaporised under the cool, blinding light of the Arahat’s gaze.

“The mango tree in Mihintale still bears fruit because its roots were planted in honest soil,” Arahat Mahinda said, turning his back on the stage with a dramatic sweep of his robes. “But this plastic garden of corruption you have built in the park will wither before the sun sets. Go back to your temples! Wash the political soot from your robes! And remember that the people of this island are no longer the naive subjects of a bygone era, they have passed the intelligence test, even if their supposed teachers have failed it miserably!”

With that final, earth-shattering declaration, the imaginary Arahat stepped away from the soiled site of the fraudulent protest.

Light that endures

Vivid figures of my daydream faded back. I returned to the dull stillness of my quiet room. The heavy sorrow that had weighed so deeply on my eighty-four-year-old heart began to lift, replaced by a gentle, enduring conviction.

The transient political circuses built by greed are nothing more than passing shadows on the ever-changing landscape of time. They do not define our beautiful island, nor can they ever truly compromise the pristine core of the Dhamma.

For twenty-three centuries, the true light brought by Arahat Mahinda has endured—not through golden fences, luxurious pageants, or the patronage of powerful politicians, but because the pristine Dhamma resides quietly and immovably within the hearts of ordinary, virtuous people.

As long as there are those who remember the simple, compassionate logic of that ancient mango tree—who seek truth, practice kindness, and guard their minds against hatred—the light of the Buddha remains undiminished. Governments rise and fall.

Interim illusions invariably crumble into dust. The timeless path of virtue stands unshakeable, offering its eternal sanctuary of peace and ultimate hope to a waiting nation. As the Blessed One declared in the Dhammapada:

 ‘Selo yathā ekaghano vātena na samīrati,

Evaṃ paṇḍitā nindāpasaṃsāsu na samiñjanti.’

“Just as a solid rock is not shaken by the storm, even so, the wise remain unmoved by praise or blame.”

title: Sri Lanka one win away from ODI Tri-Series final | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 27 October 2026 01:17
-     - 2

Haris Rauf and Shadab Khan savour the moment after Pakistan’s sensational win, Sri Lankan cricketers practice at the Gaddafi Stadium, Lahore

By Sa’adi Thawfeeq

Sri Lanka need just one win from their remaining two matches to secure a place in the Pakistan ODI Tri-Series final, where unbeaten Pakistan awaits.

Pakistan have already sealed their spot with three wins from three, while England are winless and are on the brink of elimination.

Sri Lanka meets Pakistan in a second round league match at the Gaddafi Cricket Stadium today and a win will seal their spot in the final regardless of the result of their final league game against England on Thursday.

Sri Lanka’s first meeting with Pakistan ended in a 37-run defeat. It was a match which they should have won, but for a lack of common-sense thinking on the part of their batsmen, they lost it. Since then Sri Lanka have come back strongly with a sensational two-wicket win against England chasing down a record score of 430.

That win should certainly inspire Sri Lanka to push for a win against Pakistan at a venue which is of historic importance. It was here exactly 30 years ago that Sri Lanka cricket came of age when they won the Cricket World Cup beating Australia in the final.

For England without a win after three matches to have any chance of qualifying for the final, they will need Pakistan to beat Sri Lanka in today’s game and then they must defeat Sri Lanka in their final league match. Net run rate will then decide who qualifies for the final.  

What a memorable ODI Tri-Series this is turning out to be. First it was Sri Lanka chasing down 430 - the second highest chase in ODI history. On Monday, it was England who scored 400+ in their last game and despite being kept under 250, looked like sure winners, only to see the game snatched away in the most unbelievable manner – Pakistan winning by one wicket.

Shadab Khan did the unthinkable. Under intense pressure, with Haris Rauf holding one end, Shadab single-handedly snatched a victory that no one thought was possible. A record last wicket partnership of 89 where Rauf’s contribution was only 7, and the rest was all Shadab’s. In a knock for all ages Shadab scored 113* off 96 balls (13 fours, 5 sixes) creating history on the way to the highest score ever by a number 8 batter in ODI cricket.

It was the 79th instance in ODI cricket history that a team has won a match by one wicket. Sri Lanka has been involved in four of them – 1999 v England, 2010 v Australia, 2015 v West Indies, 2020 v West Indies, and Pakistan in nine.

“It would be nice if these experiences were winning games…” said England’s white ball head coach Brendon McCullum. He admitted that his team needed to improve after three successive defeats, leaving them on the brink of elimination.

“We’ve been open to admit we need to get better and get experience into these guys,” McCullum said, reflecting on England’s inability to close out matches from promising positions. “It would be nice if these experiences were winning games from positions like we’ve found ourselves in the last three. But it’s not the case.”

“The boys are gutted, they were gutted after the last game and they are more gutted after this one. Fought so hard for so long, found a way to be put under pressure again. We have a game in a couple of days’ time, another opportunity to try and win a game for England.”

With next winter’s ODI World Cup approaching, McCullum’s plans for England will face serious questions. There is still time to address the weaknesses, but the recent defeats have exposed problems that cannot be ignored.

summary:

Mercedes’s Kimi Antonelli celebrates on the podium after winning the US Formula One Grand Prix at the Circuit of the Americas in Austin, Texas, on Sunday

Italian wunderkind Kimi Antonelli took another step toward his first Formula One championship by claiming his ninth race of the year at the United States Grand Prix in Austin, Texas.

Antonelli, 20, capitalised on his pole position and sailed to a time of 1:35:16.650 at the Circuit of the Americas on Sunday, beating Charles Leclerc of Monaco by a comfortable 13.078 seconds.

With five races to go, Antonelli does not have the championship wrapped up quite yet, but his lead over Mercedes teammate George Russell of Great Britain expanded to 123 points.

Russell must win the next race in Mexico City to remain in contention for the championship; otherwise, it will go to Antonelli, who has come to dominate the sport in his second F1 campaign.

Antonelli won five Grands Prix in a row early this season, one of which was the Miami Grand Prix. He is now 2-for-2 in the United States this season, with the Las Vegas Grand Prix still to come in November.

Max Verstappen, the four-time F1 champion for Red Bull Racing, rounded out the podium 17.485 seconds behind Antonelli. After rattling off every championship from 2021 to 2024, Verstappen has been mathematically eliminated from this year’s chase and will go two years without a world title.

The victory on Sunday also helped the Kazakh take a big step towards securing the year-end number one ranking, further burnishing a spectacular season in which she won the Australian Open title before adding the US Open crown to reach the summit.

Top seed Rybakina made the breakthrough with her trademark power in the fifth game and then unleashed a searing crosscourt backhand winner to go 4-2 up, before the 27-year-old wrapped up the opening set in only 38 minutes.

Kylian Mbappe struck twice to earn Jose Mourinho’s Real Madrid a 2-1 El Clasico victory over La Liga leaders Barcelona at Camp Nou, cutting the gap to three points.

French superstar Mbappe opened the scoring before half-time on Sunday, then slotted home late on to inflict Barca’s first domestic defeat of the campaign after Raphinha had equalised for the champions.

Real Madrid remain third, behind Atletico Madrid and Hansi Flick’s Barca, who had won their first nine games before a chastening week.

The Catalans suffered a second straight defeat after losing against Paris Saint-Germain  last week in the Champions League.

Barca won six of the seven previous Clasicos since the German arrived, but were surprisingly subdued against Mourinho’s side.

Los Blancos, without suspended winger Vinicius Junior, won their fifth straight game across all competitions, and are finding their footing under veteran Portuguese coach Mourinho.

After two trophyless seasons, Madrid turned back to Mourinho to try to stop Barca’s dominance, and this result will give them hope they are on the right track.
